articles.description:
Herodotus wrote of a bird that lived five hundred years in Arabia, and when its life came to an end, it did not wait to be surprised by death. It built its own nest of cinnamon and myrrh, set the nest and itself alight, and let a new bird rise from what the fire left behind.
The Hestia argued for tending a fire that must never go out. That’s true, and it isn’t the whole truth. Teams end. People leave. Companies get acquired, reorganized, shut down, and five years from now some part of this whole model will probably look as dated as the practices it was written to replace. No amount of tending prevents that.
Pretending otherwise is its own kind of Alexandria, a slow decline dressed up as continuity, right up until the fire goes out anyway and nobody chose the moment. The bird in Herodotus d…

Most people think the SDET title means you are automatically more valuable than a manual tester.
The SDET writes Playwright scripts. The SDET configures CI pipelines. The SDET talks about page objects and retry strategies. The manual tester clicks through screens and writes bug reports.
Here is the truth I have watched play out across teams: the manual tester who can write a SQL join will consistently outperform the SDET who cannot.
Not because SQL is magic. Because SQL is the shortest path to understanding what the system actually stores, not what the UI shows you.

articles.description:
Auditing a Solana program isn't about reading every line top to bottom and hoping something jumps out. It's about knowing the small set of places where Anchor programs actually go wrong and checking each one deliberately. This guide walks through that process in the order an experienced reviewer would follow, and ends with a checklist you can paste into your review notes.
Anchor does a lot of validation for you — but only when you use its typed accounts and constraints. Most Anchor vulnerabilities are places where the author quietly opted out of that protection. So a large part of auditing an Anchor program is finding where the safety rails were removed.
Before reading any logic, list every instruction and answer one question for each: who is allowed to call this, and how is that enforced?…

articles.author: Aeternexus Inc.
articles.description:
If you are a remote developer or an indie hacker, you probably know the feeling: You take your laptop, go to a local coffee shop or a coworking space to escape the isolation of your home office. 
You sit there for 4 hours, typing away. You look around and see three other people with MacBooks, VS Code open, clearly working on something cool. But you never say hi. Why? Because interrupting someone with headphones on feels like a crime in the developer world. 😅
I realized that we are missing out on massive opportunities—finding a technical co-founder, a beta tester, or just a friend to debug with—simply because we don't know the intent of the person sitting next to us.
So, I decided to fix this and built TogetLink.
Think of it as a low-pressure, high-intent radar for professional networking. 
Instead of swiping on LinkedIn, you physically go to a workspace (like a local cafe, WeWork, or Kolektif House) and "check-in" on the platform. You set a simple status:
🔴 "Heads down coding, don't disturb."
🟢 "Building a SaaS MVP, open to chat/brainstorm over coffee!"
Suddenly, that stranger sitting across the room isn't just a stranger anymore. You know exactly what they are working on and if they are open to collaborating. 
We call this Phygital Networking. It brings the efficiency of digital matchmaking into the real world. As developers, we love building local community hubs, but we often lack the tools to actually connect when we are physically in them.
I just launched the beta version. It's heavily focused on the developer and startup ecosystem right now. If you are tired of building in isolation, I'd love for you to create a profile and do your first check-in.
I'm also actively looking for feedback on the UX and the overall concept. 
Do you think a tool like this would make you more likely to say hi to a fellow dev in a coffee shop? 
Would you use this to find a co-founder?
Let me know in the comments! 👇
articles.title: I was tired of coding alone in cafes, so I built a "radar" to find other developers nearby.
